//: Lighthouse CI against a production build with the reference device's throttling (Phase 10d).
The numbers come from docs/CAPACITY.md §8, which is where they are explained; this file is only
where they are enforced. Two pages are audited because they have different budgets: /login is the
zero-JavaScript sign-in page and the one field vitals can never see, and /judge is the public page
with real content (the language catalogue and the limits). Everything else a student reads needs a
session, and Lighthouse holds none: the first version of this file audited /problems, which simply
redirected, so all six runs measured /login twice over and said so only in the run count.
The workspace has its own budget, enforced by the `perf` Playwright project, which signs in.
throttling: the reference device is ~4x slower than the development laptop on 3 Mbps / 1 Mbps /
150 ms. Lighthouse's own 'mobile' preset is 4x CPU and 1.6 Mbps, which is harsher on the network
than campus wifi at its worst; the explicit numbers below are the ones CAPACITY.md states.
startServerCommand goes through `npx` rather than node_modules/.bin, because the bare POSIX path is
not a command on Windows, and rather than `pnpm exec`, because the globally installed pnpm on this
machine refuses to switch versions (docs/CONVENTIONS.md: always npx pnpm@9.15.9). Both were found by
running this file locally; neither would have been found on a machine nobody has.
The assertion list carries no comment key: a `//` inside `assertions` is read as an AUDIT and fails
with 'failure for auditRan'. `no-unload-listeners` and `render-blocking-resources` are gone for the
same kind of reason — neither produces a value under these settings, so asserting on them fails on
the assertion rather than on the page. Every one of those was found by running this locally.
The budgets themselves: CAPACITY.md §8 sets LCP <= 2.0 s and CLS <= 0.1; TBT stands in for INP,
which Lighthouse cannot measure in a lab.
A separate CI job from the axe one on purpose: Lighthouse is slow and flaky under contention, and
a flaky gate sharing a job with the accessibility gate makes people re-run both.
Per URL, because the two pages are different documents and one budget for both would either
excuse /login or condemn /judge. Measured locally on 2026-10-20 (3 runs each, production build,
4x CPU / 3 Mbps / 150 ms, a loaded development laptop):
/login   LCP 1,212 ms   FCP   912 ms   CLS 0   TBT  43 ms   perf 98
/judge   LCP 2,376 ms   FCP 1,532 ms   CLS 0   TBT 277 ms   perf 91
So /login keeps CAPACITY.md's 2.0 s and /judge gets 2.5 s, for the same reason the statement page
has 2.5 s there: it is a long server-rendered document (the whole language catalogue, the limits
and the verdict table), and the number that matters for it is whether the text arrives, not
whether it beats the dashboard. The adjustment is written into docs/CAPACITY.md §8 as well; a
budget loosened without a reason in that document is a budget nobody chose.
speed-index is a WARNING on purpose: its spread on this machine was 1,973-9,141 ms across six
runs of the same page, which measures the laptop rather than the build.
